(p-5076) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾

﴿Sad﴾ is with a sukun because of pausal stopping (waqf). It has also been read with a kasra and with a fatha. It is the name of the surah, according to the view we find most convincing, regarding it and its counterparts, for the reasons we have mentioned more than once. It has also been said that it is a symbolic oath (qasam ramzi), and al-Mahayimi inclined to this view. He said: Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, swore by the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), which everyone acknowledged even before he claimed prophethood, to the point that the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn) confirmed him in his reports of unseen matters, which indicates the truthfulness of his prophetic claim; or by his purity from base morals and foul deeds, which indicates his freedom from the flaw of lying; or by his ascent through the stages of perfection, which indicates his ascent through the stages of nearness to Allah; or by his perfect patience, which is among the requirements of the message, as evidence that he is a messenger. End of quotation.

﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾: that is, full of honour (al-sharaf), which indicates its reality and truthfulness, or full of admonition (al-tadhkir), like the verse: ﴿We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10]. The response (jawab) to the oath is omitted, the context indicating it; that is, "Indeed, it is true." And his saying:

[2] ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾

﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾, i.e., pride, ﴿and opposition﴾, i.e., enmity towards the truth and submission to it. This is a turning away (idrab, a change of direction) from what precedes it, as if it were said: there is no doubt about it whatsoever, and the disbelievers' failure to believe in it is not due to any admixture of doubt in it; rather, they are in jahili (pre-Islamic ignorance) zealotry and far-reaching opposition to Allah and His Messenger. For this reason they do not submit to it. It has also been said: the answer is what the turning-away sentence indicates, i.e., those who disbelieve in it do so because of a flaw they found in it. ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. Then He threatened them for their opposition with His saying, exalted is He:

[3] ﴿How many generations did We destroy before them, and they cried out, but it was no time for escape.﴾

"How many generations did We destroy before them" — meaning: because of their arrogance towards the truth and their enmity towards its people. "And they cried out" — meaning: they called out and sought help. "But it was no time for escape" — meaning: the time was not a time for flight, for fleeing, or for deliverance. The discussion of "lāta" (lā, the negative particle) and its origin, its government (its grammatical effect), stopping on it, and joining the "tā'" (ت) to it or separating it from it, is extensively set out in the lengthier works of Arabic grammar, and in most of the tafsirs here.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[6] ﴿And the eminent ones among them went forth, saying: "Walk on, and be steadfast in your gods. Indeed, this is a thing that is intended."﴾

﴿And the eminent ones among them went forth﴾ — i.e., the nobles of Quraysh, urging one another to cling to idolatry (p-5078), and counseling one another to be patient in their rebellion, saying: ﴿Walk on﴾, i.e., in the way of your fathers; ﴿and be steadfast in your gods﴾, i.e., in worshipping them, whatever you hear of the disparaging of our minds and the refuting of our claims; ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾ — an explanation for the command to be patient: i.e., it is intended of us that we carry it through and refute it without doubt; that is, Muhammad intends it without any diverting force turning him aside or any compassion holding him back, and it is not merely a statement uttered by the tongue. Or the meaning is: indeed, this matter is one of the calamities of time, intended for us, i.e., upon us, so there is no escape for us from it, and nothing remains for us but to hold fast to it through patience.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[7] ﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion. This is nothing but a fabrication.﴾

﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion﴾ means: We have not heard of this monotheism to which you are being called in the religion of the Christians, for they are trinitarians and not monotheists; or [it means] in the religion of the Quraysh, upon which we found our fathers. ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ means: this monotheism is nothing but a pure fabrication, having no basis other than this remembrance (dhikr), according to their claim.

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[8] ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us? Nay, they are in doubt about My Reminder. Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ That is: although among us are those who are wealthier and higher in leadership. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said: They denied that he should be singled out for honour from among their nobles and leaders, and that the Book should be sent down to him from among them, as they said: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. This denial is an expression of what their hearts boiled with of envy, at the nobility of prophethood that had been bestowed upon one of their own. ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about My Reminder.﴾ This is a turning away (idrab) from an implied premise; that is: their denial of the Reminder is not based on knowledge (p. 5079), rather they are in doubt about it, saying to themselves: "Perhaps it is so, and perhaps it is not." ﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ That is: while they persist in denial. When they taste it, the doubt and envy that they have will leave them, and they will believe; but their belief will not benefit them at that time, because they will have believed out of compulsion.

Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munayyir) said in (al-Intisaf): It is derived from this that *lamma* (not yet) is appropriate to the answer. It is used to negate an action that is expected to occur, as Sibawayh says. The difference between it and *lam* (not) is that *lam* negates an action expected to occur, which does not accept *qad* (indeed) before its affirmative form; whereas *lamma* negates what is expected to occur, and may be followed by *qad* in its affirmative form.

He also said: I mention this because I was recently engaged in research on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The right of pre-emption (shuf'a) applies to what has not been divided." I had inferred from it that the right of pre-emption is specific to that which accepts division. It was said to me: its full implication is that it establishes pre-emption in what it has negated division from, so either because it does not accept division, or because it accepts it but division has not taken place. I refuted that by saying that the particle of negation mentioned here is *lam*, and its requirement is that the subject accepts the negated action and that its occurrence is expected. Do you not see that you say: "The stone does not speak"? If you said: "The stone did not speak," it would be a crude expression, because it implies that it accepts speech. End of quotation. It is subtle and excellent.

[10] ﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them ascend by the means.﴾

﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them ascend by the means.﴾ That is: let them climb up the ladders that lead them to the heaven, and let them dispose, as they wish, of the lordly affairs and the divine arrangements. (p-5080)

Ibn Jarir narrated with his chain of transmission from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "The means (asbab) are finer than hair and stronger than iron, and they are in every place, except that they are not seen." End of quotation.

This explanation corresponds to what is known as the ether (al-athir) present in the parts of the void, which is supposed to be empty. So reflect.

Then Ibn Jarir said: The root of "sabab" (means) among the Arabs is everything by which one is connected to the attainment of a goal, such as a rope, a means, a kinship, a relationship, a path, a road, and other such things. End of quotation.

Al-Muhaymini said: That is: let them ascend by the means, which are the ladders of access to the Throne, so that they may sit upon it, and thereby manage the world and send down revelation to whomever they wish. But how could they do that?

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted be He:**

[11] ﴿A host, defeated there, of the factions.﴾

﴿A host﴾ means: they are a contemptible host. ﴿Defeated there of the factions﴾ means: those who used to band together against the prophets before you, and they were overpowered and destroyed. Likewise these (will be). So do not be concerned with what they say, nor care about what they babble. And ﴿there﴾ (*hunālika*) is an indication of the place where they put themselves in the business of pursuing such speech, so it is a metaphor (*majāz*). It is also permitted that it be literal, indicating the place of their saying, which is Makkah. Qatadah said: God promised him, while he was in Makkah on that day, that He would defeat a host of the polytheists. So its fulfilment came on the Day of Badr.

Ibn Kathir said: this verse is like His saying, majestic is His greatness: ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united body that will be victorious"?﴾ [al-Qamar: 44] ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs.﴾ [al-Qamar: 45] And that was on the Day of Badr.

There are several aspects of grammar (*i'rāb*, grammatical analysis) in the verse, which al-Samin (al-Samin al-Halabi) pointed out in his words: ﴿*jundun*﴾ (a host) admits two possibilities.

The first, and the apparent one, is that it is the predicate of a subject, meaning: they are a host. And ﴿*mā*﴾ in it has two possibilities: the first is that it is superfluous (*zā'ida*). The second is that it is a qualifier of *jundun*, in the sense of magnification, for mockery of them, or for belittling them. For *mā*, when it is a qualifier, is used for these two meanings.

And ﴿*hunālika*﴾ admits three possibilities:

The first: that it is the predicate of *jundun*, with *mā* being superfluous, and ﴿*mahzūmun*﴾ (defeated) being an adjective of *jundun*.

The second: that it is a qualifier of *jundun*.

The third: that it is in the accusative governed by ﴿*mahzūmun*﴾. And ﴿*mahzūmun*﴾ also admits two possibilities: the first is that it is a second predicate of that presumed subject, and the second is that it is a qualifier of *jundun*. And ﴿*hunālika*﴾ refers to the place of the dispute and the exchange of words in the preceding sayings, which is Makkah; that is: they will be defeated in Makkah, and this is a report of the unseen. It has been said that it refers to the victory of Islam. It has also been said that it refers to the digging of the trench (al-Khandaq), meaning the place of that.

The second of the first two possibilities is that *jundun* is the subject, *mā* is superfluous, ﴿*hunālika*﴾ is an adjective, and ﴿*mahzūmun*﴾ is its predicate. But this is far-fetched, because it is detached from the speech that precedes it. End of quotation.

**Benefit:**

Ibn Abbas narrated regarding this verse that when Abu Talib fell ill, a group of Quraysh entered upon him, among them Abu Jahl, and they said: "Your nephew insults our gods, and does this and does that, and says this and says that. So if only you would send for him and forbid him!" So he sent for him. The Prophet (ﷺ) came and entered the house, and between them and Abu Talib was the space of one man's seat. He said: Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him, feared that if he sat next to Abu Talib, he (Abu Talib) would become more tender toward him. So he sprang up and sat in that seat. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) found no seat near his uncle, so he sat by the door. Abu Talib said to him: "O my nephew! What is the matter with your people, who complain about you? They claim that you insult their gods, and say this and say that." He said, and they had much to say to him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke and said: "O uncle! I want them to adopt one word which they will say, by which the Arabs will submit to them, and by which the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya (poll tax)." So they were alarmed at his word and his statement. The people said: "One word? Yes, by your father, ten!" They said: "And what is it?" Abu Talib said: "And what word is it, O my nephew?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "*Lā ilāha illā Allāh*" (There is no god but Allah). So they stood up alarmed, shaking their garments, saying: (p-5082) ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad: 5]. And the verse was revealed.

Narrated by Ibn Jarir, Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good).

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[12] ﴿Before them denied the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, lord of the stakes.﴾

﴿Before them﴾, i.e., before Quraysh: ﴿the people of Noah, and ʿĀd﴾, who are the people of Hud. ﴿Pharaoh, lord of the stakes﴾, i.e., of the firm kingdom (al-mulk al-thābit). Its origin is the tent that is fastened with ropes (aṭnāb, i.e., its cords) to its stakes (awtād). This was used for kingship as an explicit metaphor (istiʿārah taṣrīḥiyyah), and Pharaoh was described with it as hyperbole, by making him the very essence of his kingship. Alternatively, Pharaoh is likened, in the firmness of his kingdom, to the owner of a firm tent whose pillar is erected and whose stakes are driven in, by way of the implicit metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah), and what belongs to the tent's properties is attributed to him figuratively (takhyīlan), namely his saying ﴿lord of the stakes﴾, for it is a necessary attribute of the tent. Or it is a metonymy (kināyah), in that the necessary attribute is mentioned while the thing it entails is intended, which is the firm kingdom. This usage appears in the words of al-Aswad, one of the poets of the pre-Islamic age:

"And indeed they enjoyed therein the most pleasant of lives, in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firm."

Or the meaning is: lord of the great armies, so named because some of them strengthen others, as a stake strengthens a building. In that case the metaphor in "stakes" is explicit (taṣrīḥiyyah). Or it is a free metonymic figure (majāz mursal) because stakes are necessarily associated with soldiers. Or it is to be taken in its literal sense, and what is meant is the great structures and the lofty, firm edifices, and the expression is true in all of these senses.

[13] ﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the thicket. Those are the factions.﴾

﴿And Thamud﴾, who are the people of Salih. ﴿And the people of Lot and the companions of the thicket﴾, i.e., al-Ghaydah (the thicket), who are the people of Shu'ayb. ﴿Those are the factions﴾, i.e., the disbelievers who banded together against their messengers, of whom the defeated army was made up.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verse 14:**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[14] ﴿Indeed, each one of them was not but one who denied the messengers, so My punishment became due.﴾

﴿Indeed, each one of them was not but one who denied the messengers, so My punishment became due.﴾ That is: My punishment became obligatory for them. Al-Shihab said: *in* (إنْ) is negative, and *kull* (كُلٌّ) has an omitted predicate. The *tafrigh* (exclusive construction, where the element after *illa* is the only one left out from a general category) is from the most general of the general: that is, every one of them is described as nothing but one who denied all the messengers, because each of the messengers confirms all the others. So the denial of one of them is a denial of all of them. Or it is an instance of *muqabalat al-jam' bil-jam'* (matching a plural with a plural), so that each one denied his own messenger. Or it is restriction for emphasis, as if all their other attributes, in relation to this one, are as nothing, so they are overcome by it. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: In the repetition of the denial, and its clarification after its vagueness, and the variation in repeating it, first with the declarative sentence and second with the exceptive sentence, and what is in the exceptive form of restriction and specification for the sake of emphasis, there are kinds of intensification that record against them the deserving of the most severe and most forceful punishment.

Al-Nasir added another benefit of the repetition: when the discourse grew long with the enumeration of the individual deniers, and then mention of the punishment that befell them as a recompense for their denial was intended, this was repeated together with the added element mentioned, so that it would come immediately before His words ﴿so My punishment became due﴾, by way of the customary *tatriyah* (a rhetorical device of restating or bringing back a key element to refresh the listener's attention) when discourse is long. This is as I mentioned earlier concerning His words ﴿and Musa was denied﴾ [al-Hajj: 44], where the verb was repeated so that it would be linked with His words ﴿then I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Hajj: 44]. End of quotation.

The discussion concerning His words, Exalted is He:

[15] ﴿And these people await but a single Cry, with no respite (fawaq).﴾

﴿And these people await﴾ — that is, the people of Makkah — ﴿but a single Cry﴾, meaning a single seizing with a grievous punishment (p-5084). It is said: "The time (al-zaman) cried out against them" when they were destroyed, as one poet said:

"The time cried out against the family of Barmak with a cry; from its severity they fell on their chins."

Its origin is from the raid: when it overtakes a people unexpectedly and the cry falls upon them. ﴿With no respite (ma laha min fawaq)﴾ — that is, without any pause of the length of a fawaq, which is the interval between two milkings, or a return and repetition; for in it the milk returns to the udder. The word ﴿fawaq﴾ (with fatha) may be read as a verbal noun of "aafa al-mareed" (the sick person recovered), meaning ifaqah and fawaqah, when he returned to health; and with a damma it is the name of the time when milk returns to the udder. It is also read with a damma, and both are dialectal forms.

[16] ﴿And they say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) [of punishment] before the Day of Reckoning."﴾

[17] ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud (David), the one of strength.﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verse 22:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿When they entered upon Dawud, and he was frightened of them, they said, "Fear not. Two litigants: one of us has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth, and do not exceed the bounds, and guide us to the even path."﴾

﴿When they entered upon Dawud, and he was frightened of them, they said, "Fear not"﴾ i.e., of us. For we are not assailants; rather, we are ﴿two litigants﴾, i.e., two persons in dispute, who have come to you for judgment. ﴿One of us has wronged the other﴾, i.e., transgressed. ﴿So judge between us with truth﴾, i.e., with that which accords with the command of Allah. ﴿And do not exceed the bounds﴾, i.e., do not stray far from the truth or go beyond it. ﴿And guide us to the even path﴾, i.e., in such a way that you do not deviate from the truth at all.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[23] ﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. So he said, "Entrust it to me," and he overpowered me in speech.﴾

﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes﴾, i.e., female sheep of the flock (ḍa'n). ﴿And I have one ewe﴾ (p-5087), i.e., he did not consider his own wealth in respect of it, nor my need for it, but intended to overpower me. ﴿So he said, "Entrust it to me"﴾, i.e., "Make it my charge (takful) for me," meaning: make me its guardian (kāfil) just as I guard what is under my hand. Or it means: make it my share (kifl), i.e., my portion. ﴿And he overpowered me in speech﴾, i.e., he got the better of me in the discourse.

**The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:**

[24] ﴿He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes. Indeed, many of the partners (*al-khulata'*, close associates who share affairs) oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And David thought that We had tried him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance.﴾

[25] ﴿So We forgave him that. Indeed, for him with Us is a nearness and a good return.﴾

﴿He said﴾: that is, David. ﴿He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe﴾: that is, by asking for your ewe, which you were in greater need of, ﴿to be added to his ewes﴾: that is, although he had no need of this addition. ﴿Indeed, many of the partners﴾: that is, the brothers and friends who mix in their affairs. ﴿oppress one another﴾: that is, the oppression of enemies, although it is their duty toward one another to be just at the least, if they do not attain the virtue of generosity (*al-iythar*). ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: that is, they do not oppress. ﴿and few are they﴾: that is, they are few. Here *mā* is redundant (*mazīdah*), serving to express vagueness and to show wonder at their scarcity.

Al-Shihab said: In this there is exaggeration in several respects: describing them as few, the indefiniteness of *qalīl* (few), and the addition of the vague *mā*. When something is exaggerated, it becomes a basis for wonder at it, as if it were said: "How few they are!"

In this judgment of his, peace be upon him, is wisdom and decisive speech that stirs hearts and gladdens the eye of the wronged. It was a declaration of the truth in the most eloquent manner: he openly proclaimed the wrongdoing and oppression of his adversary, plainly, without favoritism or evasion, and so gladdened the eye of the oppressed. The transgressor came to know his injustice and his unfairness, and that the sword of justice and equity is above him. Then he relieved the heart of the afflicted oppressed one and eased his breast by mentioning that most people are upon this trait, the trait of oppression and lack of fairness, despite the mixing and the friendship, so that he might find solace and consolation, as it has been said: "Indeed, consolation is the spirit of every grieving one." Then he confirmed the matter by the scarcity of those who fulfill the rights of brotherhood among those who believe and do righteous deeds; so how about others? All of these are wise sayings, precious pearls and truths that apply to most of this great multitude of people who claim love and friendship.

Because of the great importance of the rights of love, the scholars of ethics (*'ulamā' al-akhlāq*) expanded greatly on its etiquettes, varying their chapters and coloring their sections. Yet complaints remain widespread. The books of literature have been filled with its verse and prose, as is not hidden from one who has familiarity with it. And success is from Allah.

﴿And David thought that We had tried him﴾: that is, We tested him with that legal case. ﴿and he fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾. ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ [25]: that is, what he asked forgiveness for. ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness﴾ [25]: that is, closeness. ﴿and a good return﴾ [25]: that is, a good place of return and honor in the Hereafter.

**Notes (tanbīhāt):**

The first: The exegetes (*al-mufassirūn*, practitioners of tafsir, i.e., Qur'anic exegesis) have many opinions and varied views on this narrative. They return to two positions: the position of those who see that it allusively points to a sin that befell David, peace be upon him, and for which he was forgiven; and the position of those who see that it is a legal case between two disputants, with no implication of that. Among those who took the first view is Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari). He said: This is a parable that the two litigants who scaled David's sanctuary (*miḥrāb*) set forth. The reason is that David had, it is said, ninety-nine wives, and the man whom he had sent on a campaign until he was killed had only one wife. When he was killed, David married his wife, it is mentioned. Then, when he judged between the two disputants with what he judged, he knew that he had been tested. So he asked forgiveness for his sin, fell down prostrating to Allah, turned toward the pleasure of his Lord, and repented of his error. This is what Ibn Jarir said. Then he traced his lengthy narrative through reports from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Qatadah, Wahb, and Mujahid, and through a chain from Anas traced to the Prophet. Some of its wording resembles what is mentioned in the Torah as it is circulated today.

Al-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil*: The story they recount concerning the woman, that she pleased him, and that he sent her husband out with a military expedition until he was killed, was transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim from a hadith of Anas traced to the Prophet. Its chain includes Ibn Lahi'a, whose condition is well known, from Ibn Sakhr, from Yazid al-Raqqashi, who is weak. He also transmitted it from a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of a companion (*mawqūf*). End of quotation.

I say: As for the report traced to the Prophet, peace be upon him, in it, it has not come through any sound chain. As for what is reported as a statement of the Companions and Successors, may Allah be pleased with them, their reliance in this is what is mentioned in the Torah about this narrative, or trust in the one who related it from them. From this follows their inclination to permit such a thing for the prophets. Some have permitted everything except lying in conveying the message, as is explained in the lengthier works.

Ibn Hazm, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the view of the Karramiyya among the Murji'ah, of Ibn al-Tayyib al-Baqillani among the Ash'ariyyah, and of those who follow him, and it is the view of the Jews and Christians. Then he refuted this view, may Allah have mercy on him, with a firm refutation.

As for the second position, it is what Ibn Hazm definitively held in *al-Fisal*, and his words are: What Allah, Exalted is He, related about David, peace be upon him, is a true and sound statement, not indicating anything of what the lying mockers have said, who cling to fables fabricated by the Jews. That litigant was, without doubt, people from the children of Adam, disputing over ewes of sheep in reality among themselves. One of them transgressed against the other, according to the text of the verse. Whoever says they were angels alluding to the matter of women has lied against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and attributed to Him what He did not say, and added to the Qur'an what is not in it, and called Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, a liar, and confessed against his own wicked self that he called the angels liars. For Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ [38:21]. He said: They were never two disputants, nor did one of them transgress against the other, nor did one of them have ninety-nine ewes while the other had only one ewe, nor did he say to him, "Entrust it to me." So wonder! Why do they insert falsehood into it of their own accord? We seek refuge in Allah from abandonment. Moreover, all of that is without evidence; it is mere bare claim. By Allah! Each one of us protects himself and his concealed neighbor from desiring his neighbor's wife and then deliberately exposing her husband to death so as to marry her, and from abandoning his prayer for a bird he sees. These are the deeds of foolish, dissolute, rebellious sinners, not the deeds of the people of righteousness and piety.

How then about the Messenger of Allah David, peace be upon him, to whom He revealed His Book and upon whose tongue He made His speech flow? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has exalted him above such obscenity crossing his mind. How then could it be attributed to his deeds? As for his seeking forgiveness, his falling down prostrating, and Allah's forgiveness of him, the prophets, peace be upon them, are the most worthy of these noble deeds.

Seeking forgiveness is a good act that is not rejected from an angel or a prophet, nor from a sinner or one who is not a sinner. The Prophet seeks forgiveness from Allah for the sinners of the earth. And the angels, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire."﴾ [40:7]

As for His saying, Exalted is He, about David, peace be upon him: ﴿And David thought that We had tried him﴾, David, peace be upon him, thought that what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had given him of the vast extent of sovereignty might be a trial. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, used to supplicate that Allah make his heart firm upon His religion. So he sought forgiveness from Allah, Exalted is He, for this thought, and Allah, Exalted is He, forgave him this thought, since what Allah, Exalted is He, had given him of that was not a trial. End of Ibn Hazm's words. This is a stopping at the apparent meaning of the verse, devoid of any allusion or hint.

Al-Burhan al-Biqa'i said in his *Tafsir*: That story and its like are among the lies of the Jews.

Then he said: Some of those among them who embraced Islam informed me that they deliberately do this regarding David, peace be upon him, because 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, is from his descendants, so that they might find a way to slander him. End of quotation.

Then he said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ [38:25] refers to falling into speech about attributing injustice to someone without hearing his statement. This claim is a training for David, peace be upon him, in judgments.

Mentioning it to the Prophet, peace be upon him, is a training for him in patience (*al-anāh*) in all his affairs continuously. When he mentioned this, it perhaps gave the impression of something affecting his station, peace be upon him, so He dispelled it with His saying: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness and a good return﴾ [38:25]. The story was mentioned only for elevation in the degrees of perfection. The first evidence for what I have mentioned is that this trial was only a training in judgment, not regarding a woman or anything else. And what they mentioned about the story of the woman is false, even if it is widely known. How many a widely known falsehood and widely cited report is nothing but pure fabrication! End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: The exegetes have mentioned here a story most of which is taken from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives traced to Jewish and Christian sources). No hadith from the infallible one (the Prophet) that must be followed has been established concerning it. However, Ibn Abi Hatim related here a hadith whose chain is not sound, because it is from the narration of Yazid al-Raqqashi from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him. Yazid, although he was among the righteous, is weak in hadith according to the imams. The best course is to restrict oneself to merely reciting this story and to leave its knowledge to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the Qur'an is true, and whatever it contains is true as well. End of quotation.

Qadi 'Iyad said in *al-Shifa*: As for the story of David, peace be upon him, it is not necessary to pay attention to what the historians (*al-akhbāriyyūn*) wrote about it, based on the People of the Book who altered and changed, and which some exegetes transmitted, though Allah did not specify anything of that, nor was it reported in a sound hadith.

What Allah specified is His saying: ﴿And David thought that We had tried him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance﴾, and His saying about him: "awwāb" (one who returns repeatedly). The meaning of ﴿fatannāhu﴾ is: We tested him. As for "awwāb," Qatadah said: obedient. And this interpretation is better. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: David said nothing more than to the man: "Step down from your wife and entrust her to me." So Allah rebuked him for that and alerted him to it, and denounced his preoccupation with worldly matters. This is what should be relied upon regarding his affair. It has been said that he proposed to her after his (the other's) proposal, and it has been said: rather, he desired in his heart that he be martyred.

Al-Samarqandi related that the sin for which he sought forgiveness was his saying: ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾, so he wronged him by the words of his adversary. It has also been said: rather, when he feared for himself, and considered as a trial what had been spread out before him of kingship and worldly life. To the negation of what has been attributed in the reports to David concerning that went Ahmad ibn Nasr and Abu Tammam, and others among the researchers.

Al-Dawudi said: There is no established report in the story of David and Uriah. One should not suppose that a prophet would desire the killing of a Muslim. It has been said: the two disputants who came to him were two men in the offspring of sheep, according to the apparent meaning of the verse. And it has been said: rather, when he feared for himself and considered as a trial what had been spread out for him of kingship and worldly life. End of quotation.

(p-5092) Ibn al-Qayyim said at the end of his book (al-Jawab al-Kafi), in the discussions on passionate love ('ishq): The Prophet (ﷺ) guided those who love one another to marriage, as in Sunan Ibn Majah, where it is related with a marfu' chain: "No one has seen anything like marriage for two who love each other." His marrying his beloved is the cure for passionate love, which Allah made its cure by legislation and by decree. With it the Prophet of Allah Dawud (peace be upon him) treated himself, and the Prophet of Allah did not commit a forbidden act. He married the woman and joined her to his wives only because of his love for her. His repentance was in proportion to his rank with Allah and the elevation of his station. We should not add anything to this. End of quotation.

This is his acceptance of part of the story, not all of it, and it is one of the opinions concerning it.

As for the claim of some that the Torah counts Dawud as a wise king, not a prophet, citing his mention in the Books of Kings and what is in them that a prophet named Nathan (Qashan) was sent to him and struck the parable mentioned, this claim is rejected on several grounds:

First, arguing from the Torah in their hands, either to affirm or deny, is not to be relied upon. How could it be, when we have been given a white, pure book, preserved from alteration and substitution, praise be to Allah, the Exalted?

Second, there is no disagreement among Muslims about the prophethood of Dawud (peace be upon him), so the dissent of others carries no weight.

Third, there is no barrier to kingship and prophethood being combined in one whom Allah chooses and selects. This was done with Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them both).

Fourth, our noble Book needs no completion from what came in other scriptures, nor any attempt to reduce it to other books or to refer it to them, since it is self-sufficient, and since it is the witness over all other books, as Allah the Exalted informed about it. So let this be pondered. And Allah knows best.

It is related that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz was told the account of Dawud as the storytellers (qussas) narrate it, and with him was a man from the People of Truth. He denied the narrator, and said: If the story is as it is in the Book of Allah, then it should not be sought to be otherwise, and how great is the matter when someone says otherwise. And if it is as you mention, and Allah withheld it as a veil over His Prophet, then it should not be made known to him. Umar said: Hearing this speech of yours is dearer to me than everything the sun has risen upon. Transmitted by al-Zamakhshari.

(p-5093) An-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: The verifying scholars among our imams have held that the prophets, peace be upon them, Dawud and others, are free from falling into minor sins, cleared of that, and they sought sound interpretations for such accounts. This is the clear truth and the most luminous path, if Allah the Exalted wills. End of quotation.

Second point: Ibn al-Furs said: In this story there is evidence for the permissibility of judging in the mosque (meaning in the outer part of the prayer niche, though it is not explicit regarding the niche of the mosque), and for gentleness in turning a person away from what is disliked, which he (Dawud) did, and that one should not be treated with harshness as far as possible, and the permissibility of allusive speech (ma'arid min al-qawl).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It came in the manner of parable and allusion rather than explicit statement, because it is more forceful in rebuke. For when the one reflecting is led to feel that he is being alluded to, it strikes his soul more, takes firmer hold of his heart, has greater effect on him, and better prompts his modesty and shame, and is more apt to alert him to the error, than being confronted with it openly, while observing good manners by avoiding public exposure. Do you not see how the wise advised in disciplining a child: when you find from him a shameful lapse, allude to disapproving of it rather than stating it openly? And that a story be related to him that mirrors his condition; when he reflects on it, he will find the state of the story's character foolish, and thus find his own state foolish, and that is more effective in restraining him, because it sets that as an example for his condition and a measure for his matter, so he conceives the ugliness of what occurred from him in an unveiled image, while it also better preserves what lies between parent and child from the veil of shame.

Third: Ibn Mas'ud said regarding the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾ [Sad: 23], that it means "on my religion." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it. Thus it contains the permissibility of applying the term "brother" to one who is not a close relation. And he cited the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, many of the partners⁠ [khulata'] ...﴾ as evidence for the permissibility of partnership; this was reported in al-Iklil.

Fourth: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: Whoever permits substituting bowing (ruku') for the prostration of recitation uses the words ﴿and he fell down bowing﴾ as evidence. But most scholars hold that ruku' here is a metonymy (majaz mursal) for sujud, because bowing leads to prostration, so it was treated as its cause and then used for it; or it is a metaphor (isti'arah) for it, due to their similarity in bending and humility.

Fifth: Ibn Kathir said: The imams differed over the prostration of Sad [Sad: 1], whether it is one of the obligatory prostrations (azai'm al-sujud), into two views. One of them: it is not among the obligatory ones, but is a prostration of thanks, because of what is related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both), that he said: "It is not among the obligatory prostrations, and I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrate in it," narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, and the authors of the Sunan.

And from him, that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad and said: Dawud (peace be upon him) prostrated it in repentance, and we prostrate it in thanks," related solely by al-Nasa'i.

And from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Sad while on the minbar; when he reached the prostration he came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. On another day he recited it, and when he reached the prostration the people braced themselves to prostrate. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: It is only the repentance of a prophet, but I see you have braced yourselves; so he came down and prostrated." Related solely by Abu Dawud, and its chain is according to the conditions of the Sahih.
