So he sought forgiveness from Allah, Exalted is He, for this thought, and Allah, Exalted is He, forgave him this thought, since what Allah, Exalted is He, had given him of that was not a trial. End of Ibn Hazm's words. This is a stopping at the apparent meaning of the verse, devoid of any allusion or hint.

Al-Burhan al-Biqa'i said in his *Tafsir*: That story and its like are among the lies of the Jews.

Then he said: Some of those among them who embraced Islam informed me that they deliberately do this regarding David, peace be upon him, because 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, is from his descendants, so that they might find a way to slander him. End of quotation.

Then he said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ [38:25] refers to falling into speech about attributing injustice to someone without hearing his statement. This claim is a training for David, peace be upon him, in judgments.

Mentioning it to the Prophet, peace be upon him, is a training for him in patience (*al-anāh*) in all his affairs continuously. When he mentioned this, it perhaps gave the impression of something affecting his station, peace be upon him, so He dispelled it with His saying: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness and a good return﴾ [38:25]. The story was mentioned only for elevation in the degrees of perfection. The first evidence for what I have mentioned is that this trial was only a training in judgment, not regarding a woman or anything else. And what they mentioned about the story of the woman is false, even if it is widely known. How many a widely known falsehood and widely cited report is nothing but pure fabrication! End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: The exegetes have mentioned here a story most of which is taken from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives traced to Jewish and Christian sources). No hadith from the infallible one (the Prophet) that must be followed has been established concerning it. However, Ibn Abi Hatim related here a hadith whose chain is not sound, because it is from the narration of Yazid al-Raqqashi from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him. Yazid, although he was among the righteous, is weak in hadith according to the imams. The best course is to restrict oneself to merely reciting this story and to leave its knowledge to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the Qur'an is true, and whatever it contains is true as well. End of quotation.

Qadi 'Iyad said in *al-Shifa*: As for the story of David, peace be upon him, it is not necessary to pay attention to what the historians (*al-akhbāriyyūn*) wrote about it, based on the People of the Book who altered and changed, and which some exegetes transmitted, though Allah did not specify anything of that, nor was it reported in a sound hadith.

What Allah specified is His saying: ﴿And David thought that We had tried him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance﴾, and His saying about him: "awwāb" (one who returns repeatedly). The meaning of ﴿fatannāhu﴾ is: We tested him. As for "awwāb," Qatadah said: obedient. And this interpretation is better. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: David said nothing more than to the man: "Step down from your wife and entrust her to me." So Allah rebuked him for that and alerted him to it, and denounced his preoccupation with worldly matters. This is what should be relied upon regarding his affair. It has been said that he proposed to her after his (the other's) proposal, and it has been said: rather, he desired in his heart that he be martyred.

Al-Samarqandi related that the sin for which he sought forgiveness was his saying: ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾, so he wronged him by the words of his adversary. It has also been said: rather, when he feared for himself, and considered as a trial what had been spread out before him of kingship and worldly life. To the negation of what has been attributed in the reports to David concerning that went Ahmad ibn Nasr and Abu Tammam, and others among the researchers.

Al-Dawudi said: There is no established report in the story of David and Uriah. One should not suppose that a prophet would desire the killing of a Muslim. It has been said: the two disputants who came to him were two men in the offspring of sheep, according to the apparent meaning of the verse. And it has been said: rather, when he feared for himself and considered as a trial what had been spread out for him of kingship and worldly life. End of quotation.

(p-5092) Ibn al-Qayyim said at the end of his book (al-Jawab al-Kafi), in the discussions on passionate love ('ishq): The Prophet (ﷺ) guided those who love one another to marriage, as in Sunan Ibn Majah, where it is related with a marfu' chain: "No one has seen anything like marriage for two who love each other." His marrying his beloved is the cure for passionate love, which Allah made its cure by legislation and by decree. With it the Prophet of Allah Dawud (peace be upon him) treated himself, and the Prophet of Allah did not commit a forbidden act. He married the woman and joined her to his wives only because of his love for her. His repentance was in proportion to his rank with Allah and the elevation of his station. We should not add anything to this. End of quotation.

This is his acceptance of part of the story, not all of it, and it is one of the opinions concerning it.

As for the claim of some that the Torah counts Dawud as a wise king, not a prophet, citing his mention in the Books of Kings and what is in them that a prophet named Nathan (Qashan) was sent to him and struck the parable mentioned, this claim is rejected on several grounds:

First, arguing from the Torah in their hands, either to affirm or deny, is not to be relied upon. How could it be, when we have been given a white, pure book, preserved from alteration and substitution, praise be to Allah, the Exalted?

Second, there is no disagreement among Muslims about the prophethood of Dawud (peace be upon him), so the dissent of others carries no weight.

Third, there is no barrier to kingship and prophethood being combined in one whom Allah chooses and selects. This was done with Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them both).

Fourth, our noble Book needs no completion from what came in other scriptures, nor any attempt to reduce it to other books or to refer it to them, since it is self-sufficient, and since it is the witness over all other books, as Allah the Exalted informed about it. So let this be pondered. And Allah knows best.

It is related that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz was told the account of Dawud as the storytellers (qussas) narrate it, and with him was a man from the People of Truth. He denied the narrator, and said: If the story is as it is in the Book of Allah, then it should not be sought to be otherwise, and how great is the matter when someone says otherwise. And if it is as you mention, and Allah withheld it as a veil over His Prophet, then it should not be made known to him. Umar said: Hearing this speech of yours is dearer to me than everything the sun has risen upon. Transmitted by al-Zamakhshari.

(p-5093) An-Nasir said in al-Intisaf: The verifying scholars among our imams have held that the prophets, peace be upon them, Dawud and others, are free from falling into minor sins, cleared of that, and they sought sound interpretations for such accounts. This is the clear truth and the most luminous path, if Allah the Exalted wills. End of quotation.

Second point: Ibn al-Furs said: In this story there is evidence for the permissibility of judging in the mosque (meaning in the outer part of the prayer niche, though it is not explicit regarding the niche of the mosque), and for gentleness in turning a person away from what is disliked, which he (Dawud) did, and that one should not be treated with harshness as far as possible, and the permissibility of allusive speech (ma'arid min al-qawl).

Al-Zamakhshari said: It came in the manner of parable and allusion rather than explicit statement, because it is more forceful in rebuke. For when the one reflecting is led to feel that he is being alluded to, it strikes his soul more, takes firmer hold of his heart, has greater effect on him, and better prompts his modesty and shame, and is more apt to alert him to the error, than being confronted with it openly, while observing good manners by avoiding public exposure. Do you not see how the wise advised in disciplining a child: when you find from him a shameful lapse, allude to disapproving of it rather than stating it openly? And that a story be related to him that mirrors his condition; when he reflects on it, he will find the state of the story's character foolish, and thus find his own state foolish, and that is more effective in restraining him, because it sets that as an example for his condition and a measure for his matter, so he conceives the ugliness of what occurred from him in an unveiled image, while it also better preserves what lies between parent and child from the veil of shame.

Third: Ibn Mas'ud said regarding the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾ [Sad: 23], that it means "on my religion." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted it. Thus it contains the permissibility of applying the term "brother" to one who is not a close relation. And he cited the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, many of the partners⁠ [khulata'] ...﴾ as evidence for the permissibility of partnership; this was reported in al-Iklil.

Fourth: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: Whoever permits substituting bowing (ruku') for the prostration of recitation uses the words ﴿and he fell down bowing﴾ as evidence. But most scholars hold that ruku' here is a metonymy (majaz mursal) for sujud, because bowing leads to prostration, so it was treated as its cause and then used for it; or it is a metaphor (isti'arah) for it, due to their similarity in bending and humility.

Fifth: Ibn Kathir said: The imams differed over the prostration of Sad [Sad: 1], whether it is one of the obligatory prostrations (azai'm al-sujud), into two views. One of them: it is not among the obligatory ones, but is a prostration of thanks, because of what is related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both), that he said: "It is not among the obligatory prostrations, and I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrate in it," narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, and the authors of the Sunan.

And from him, that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in Sad and said: Dawud (peace be upon him) prostrated it in repentance, and we prostrate it in thanks," related solely by al-Nasa'i.

And from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Sad while on the minbar; when he reached the prostration he came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. On another day he recited it, and when he reached the prostration the people braced themselves to prostrate. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: It is only the repentance of a prophet, but I see you have braced yourselves; so he came down and prostrated." Related solely by Abu Dawud, and its chain is according to the conditions of the Sahih.

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[ 26 ] ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah (vicegerent) upon the earth. So judge between the people in truth, and do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who stray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning.﴾.

﴿O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth﴾, i.e., We have made you a successor (istakhlafnaka) in the kingship over the earth, like one whom some sultans appoint over some lands, granting him sovereignty over them. From this comes their saying: "the khulafa' of Allah on His earth." ﴿So judge between the people in truth and do not follow desire﴾, i.e., the desire of the self, arising from inclination toward wealth, or rank, or a relative, or a companion. ﴿Lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾, i.e., His path, which leads to the perfections, such as preserving the kingdom, victory over enemies, salvation in the Hereafter, and the elevation of ranks therein. ﴿Indeed, those who stray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning﴾, i.e., because of their forgetting, which is their straying from the path. For remembering it requires adherence to the truth and opposition to desire.

Admonition:

In the verse is an explanation of the obligation to judge by the truth, and that one should not incline toward either of the two disputants because of kinship, hope of gain, or any cause that calls for inclination. Some scholars have used it as evidence that the earth needs a khalifah from Allah. So says al-Iklil. Ibn Kathir said: This is a charge from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to those in authority, that they judge between the people by the truth revealed from Him, Blessed and Exalted, and not deviate from it, lest they stray from the way of Allah. Blessed and Exalted has threatened whoever strays from His path and forgets the Day of Reckoning with a firm warning and a severe punishment.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Zur'ah that al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik said to him: "Is the caliph held to account? For you have read the earlier Book, read the Qur'an, and gained understanding." I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, may I speak?" He said: "Speak, under safe conduct." I said: "O Commander of the Faithful! Are you more honored by Allah, or David, upon him be peace? Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, gathered for him prophethood and caliphate. Then He warned him in His Book, saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth﴾," and the verse.

Al-Razi said: Know that man was created civil by nature, because a single person's interests cannot be organized except in the presence of a complete city. This one plows, that one grinds, another bakes, another weaves, and another sews. In sum, each of them is occupied with an important task, and the interests of all are organized by the works of all. Thus it is established that man is civil by nature. When they gather in one place, disputes and quarrels arise among them, and there must be a powerful, dominant person who ends those disputes and decides those judgments. That is the authority whose ruling is executed over all.

It is therefore established that the interests of creation cannot be organized except by a dominant, governing authority. Then, if that dominant governing authority's rule follows its own desire and seeks the interests of its worldly life, its harm to creation is great, for it makes its subjects a ransom for itself and uses them to achieve its own aims. This leads to the ruin of the world, the spread of chaos and disorder among creation, and ultimately to the destruction of that kingdom.

But if the rulings of that king conform to the true divine law, the interests of the world are organized and the doors of good are opened wide in the best manner. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿So judge between the people in truth﴾, i.e., there must be a judge among the people by the truth, so be you that judge. Then He said: ﴿And do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾, and the verse. Its explanation is that following desire necessitates straying from the way of Allah, and straying from the way of Allah necessitates evil punishment. Thus it follows that following desire necessitates evil punishment. End.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[27] ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve, from the Fire.﴾

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ meaning: a creation in vain, with no wisdom in it; or [it means] while acting in vain and frivolously. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38] ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39], and the truth is that people establish justice in beliefs, acts of worship, and dealings. ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ meaning: for this reason they denied the resurrection and the recompense for deeds, and they began to turn people away from the way of Allah and to seek corruption on earth.

(p-5097) Al-Zamakhshari said: Whoever denies the Creator has denied wisdom at its root, and whoever denies wisdom in the creation of the world has shown the Creator to be foolish. By this it becomes clear that he does not know Him and does not measure Him by His true measure, so his affirmation that He is the Creator is no affirmation at all.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[28] ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds the same as those who cause corruption on earth? Or shall We treat the God-fearing the same as the wicked?﴾

﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds the same as those who cause corruption on earth?﴾ Al-Muhayimi said: That is, shall We abandon resurrection altogether, or shall We resurrect and make those who believed, and who thanked the blessing of intellect and the Book, and who did righteous deeds, thanking the blessing of the limbs, the same as those who cause corruption, who divert intellect and limbs to other than what they were created for? ﴿Or shall We treat the God-fearing﴾ that is, those who avoid opposing God's command, guarding His love, ﴿the same as the wicked﴾ that is, those who oppose God's commands and do not care about His enmity. That is: We do not do that, and they are not equal in the sight of God.

Ibn Kathir said: If the matter is so, there must be another abode in which this obedient one is rewarded and this wicked one is punished. This guidance indicates to sound minds and upright natures that there must be a return and a recompense. We see the oppressive transgressor whose wealth, children and comfort increase, and who dies in that state, and we see the obedient oppressed one who dies of his grief. So there must be, in the wisdom of the All-Wise, the All-Knowing, the Just, who does not wrong even an atom's weight, a redress of this one against that one. And since this does not happen in this abode, it is necessarily established that there is another abode for this recompense and consolation. And since the Qur'an guides to the correct aims and the clear rational sources, He, exalted is He, said:

**The interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:**

[29] ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, full of blessings, that they may contemplate its verses, and that those of understanding may be reminded.﴾

﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, full of blessings﴾ — that is, abundant in good.

﴿That they may contemplate (tadabbur, reflective pondering) its verses﴾ — al-Mahayimi said: That is, that they may look into its words, their arrangement, and their implications, so that they may extract from them sciences through inference.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Tadabbur of the verses is reflecting upon them and considering them, a consideration that leads to knowing what their apparent meaning leads to of correct interpretations and fine meanings, because whoever is content with the apparent meaning of what is recited will not gain much benefit from it.

Its example is like the example of one who has a milch she-camel that yields abundant milk but he does not milk her, and a prolific mare but he does not breed her. It was also narrated from al-Hasan: Slaves and children have recited this Qur'an, having no knowledge of its interpretation. They preserved its letters and neglected its limits, to the extent that one of them would say: "By Allah, I have recited the Qur'an and I have not omitted a single letter from it," while by Allah he has omitted all of it, and no trace of the Qur'an is seen in his character or his deeds. By Allah, that is not preserving its letters while neglecting its limits. By Allah, these are not the wise, nor the men of restraint. May Allah not multiply the likes of these among people. O Allah, make us among the scholars who contemplate, and protect us from the readers who are arrogant.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿And We gave to David, Solomon. An excellent servant. Indeed, he was one who constantly turned back (to Allah).﴾

﴿And We gave to David, Solomon. An excellent servant. Indeed, he was one who constantly turned back (to Allah).﴾ That is: one who returns often to Allah, exalted is He, through repentance (tawbah) and turning back in devotion (inabah).

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[31] ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening, the poised, swift steeds.﴾

﴿When there were displayed before him at evening the poised [al-ṣāfināt]﴾ i.e., of the horses, plural of (ṣāfin), which is the one that stands on the tip of the hoof of a forefoot or a hind foot. ﴿The swift [al-jiyād]﴾ plural of (jawād), which is the one that hastens in its running; or it means the good, plural of (jayyid).

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[32] ﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good (wealth) over the remembrance of my Lord, until (the sun) was hidden behind the veil."﴾

﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good (wealth) over the remembrance of my Lord"﴾: that is, I preferred it over Him. He departed from the expected wording ('ana) for the sake of verbal correspondence (al-munasabah al-lafziyyah) and the intention of paronomasia (tajnis), and for the benefit of implicit meaning (tadmin), indicating that this love had arisen (in him) suddenly. And ﴿the remembrance of my Lord﴾ is either an annexation to its agent or to its object.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-khayr (good) means wealth, as in His saying: ﴿if he leaves behind some good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, he is intensely fond of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8]. The wealth here is the horses that occupied him. Or (the speaker) called the horses 'good' as though they were the very essence of good, because good is attached to them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Good is tied to the foreheads of horses until the Day of Resurrection." He also said, concerning Zayd al-Khayl when he came to him as a delegation and embraced Islam: "No man was described to me and I saw him but he fell short of what had reached me, except Zayd al-Khayl." And he named him Zayd al-Khayr (Zayd of good). A man asked Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, about a people racing, "Who is the one who won?" He said, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The man said to him, "I meant the horses." He said, "And I meant the good."

﴿until (the sun) was hidden behind the veil﴾: that is, the sun set. It is connected to His saying: ﴿I have preferred﴾. In it there is an explicit metaphor (isti'arah tasrihiyyah) or an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), by likening the sun to a beautiful woman or an angel. The letter ba' in ﴿behind the veil﴾ is for locative sense (zarfiyyah), or for instrument (isti'anah), or for accompaniment (mulabasah).

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[33] ﴿Bring them back to me.﴾ Then he began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks.

﴿Bring them back to me﴾ means the swift, standing steeds, and this is part of the speech itself, so there is no need to posit another speech (qawl) as implied.

﴿Then he began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks﴾ meaning: he began to pass over, that is, to pass the sword over their shanks and necks, meaning he cut them.

Note (tanbih):

Ibn Kathir said: More than one of the early authorities (salaf) and exegetes have mentioned that Sulayman, peace be upon him, became occupied with reviewing the horses until the time of the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr) had passed. What is certain is that he did not abandon it deliberately but out of forgetfulness, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was occupied on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq) from the afternoon prayer until he prayed it after sunset, and this is established in the Two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) through more than one chain. It is also possible that delaying prayer for the excuse of raiding and fighting was permissible in their religious law, since horses are kept for fighting. A group of scholars claimed that this was prescribed and was then abrogated by the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf); and among them are those who held that this applies in a state of close combat and pressing engagement, when no prayer, bowing or prostration is possible, as the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did at the conquest of Tustar; this is reported from Makhul, al-Awza'i and others. The first view, however, is closer to the truth, because He said after: ﴿Bring them back to me, then he began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks.﴾ Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He said, "No, by Allah! You shall not distract me from the worship of my Lord, the last of what is with you," then he commanded them, and they were hamstrung. Qatadah also said the same.

'Ali ibn Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: He began to pass his hand over the manes of the horses and their hamstrings, out of love for them. This view was chosen by Ibn Jarir, who said: Because he would not have punished an animal by hamstringing it, and destroyed some of his property without cause, merely because he had been distracted from his prayer by looking at them, when they were not at fault. Yet this reasoning of Ibn Jarir is open to question, because it may have been permissible in their law, especially if it was out of zeal for Allah, the Exalted, given that he had become occupied with them until the time of prayer had passed. For this reason, when he gave them up for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, compensated him with something better than them: the wind that runs at his command gently wherever he wills, whose morning course is a month's journey and whose evening course is a month's journey. This is swifter and better than horses.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Qatadah and Abu al-Dahma'—and they used to travel much toward the House—they said: We came upon a man from the desert people, and the Bedouin said to us: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, took my hand and began to teach me of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had taught him, and said: "Indeed, you do not leave anything out of fear of Allah, the Exalted, except that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives you something better than it." End of what Ibn Kathir mentioned.

al-Qashani said: That is, he began to pass the sword over their shanks, hamstringing some of them and slaughtering some of them, as a breaking of the idols of the soul which it worships through its desire, and as a suppression of its fury and its powers, and as a lifting of the veil that stands between him and the Truth, and as seeking forgiveness and turning to Him through detachment and abandonment.

al-Razi went to another interpretation, which he approved. He said: The tethering of horses was recommended in their religion, just as it is in the religion of Islam. Then Sulayman, peace be upon him, needed to make a raid, so he sat down and ordered the horses to be brought and ordered them to be paraded. He said: I do not love them for the sake of this world and the portion of the self, but I love them for the command of Allah and the seeking of strengthening His religion. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾ [Sad: 32]. Then he, peace be upon him, ordered them to be driven and moved on until they were hidden by the veil, that is, they went out of his sight. Then he ordered the trainers to bring those horses back to him. When they returned to him, he began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks. The purpose of that passing of the hand is several matters:

The first: to honor them and to show their nobility, because they are among the greatest helpers in repelling the enemy.

The second: that he wished to show that in governing the state and the kingdom he takes pains to personally handle most affairs himself.

The third: that he had greater knowledge of the conditions, diseases and defects of horses, so he would test them and pass his hand over their shanks and necks, to know whether there was anything in them indicating sickness.

He said: This interpretation that we have mentioned fits the wording of the Qur'an in an exact and corresponding way, and we are not obliged to attribute any of those objectionable and forbidden things to him.

He said: I am greatly astonished at how people accepted these foolish views, although reason and transmission reject them, and they have no doubt in establishing them, let alone proof. If it is said: The majority interpreted the verse in that manner, so what is your view of it? We say: We have here two positions:

The first position: We claim that the wording of the verse does not indicate any of those aspects they mention. It has become clear, praise be to Allah, that the matter is as we have mentioned, and no intelligent person doubts its clarity.

The second position: Suppose the wording of the verse does not indicate it, but it is a story that people have related. So what is your view of it? Our answer: Many proofs have been established for the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, and no proof has indicated the soundness of these narrations; and a single-transmission report (khabar al-ahad) is not fit to oppose strong proofs. How then about narrations from people who are not regarded and whose sayings are not heeded? And Allah knows best. End of al-Razi's words.

Ibn Hazm preceded him when he said: To interpret the verse as meaning that he killed the horses because he became occupied with them away from the prayer is a fabrication, forged, false, foolish and cold, gathering various kinds of nonsense; for in it is the punishment of horses that bear no fault, mutilating them, destroying useful property without purpose, and attributing the neglect of prayer to a messenger prophet; then he punishes the horses for his own sin, not for theirs. The meaning of the verse is rather that he informed that he loved the good out of remembrance of his Lord until the sun was hidden, or those swift steeds were behind their veil; then he commanded their return, and he began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks, showing kindness and honor to them. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, which admits of no other, and there is no allusion in it at all to what they have mentioned of killing horses and neglecting the prayer. All of this has been said by reliable Muslims. How then, when there is no proof in the word of anyone other than the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace? End of Ibn Hazm's words.

I say: What appears correct is that this story was alluded to as a report that was known to them, since the noble revelation confirms what is before it, but it has final authority over it. Whatever it stated of the details of what is before it is to be affirmed and not exceeded. In that case, the well-known story among them is what is alluded to, but under its authority, not accepted in all its particulars. And His words, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[34] ﴿And We certainly tried Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (in repentance).﴾

﴿And We certainly tried Solomon﴾, i.e., We tested him. ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body﴾, i.e., a fleshly form, as a metaphor for an idol, according to what they have related. The word "body" (jasad) was preferred over it out of reverence for Solomon, peace be upon him, and as an indication that his story, if it is authentic, was a matter that occurred and then passed away. This is shown by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then he turned back﴾, i.e., to his Lord in repentance and seeking forgiveness, as He clarified with His words, glorified is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

[35] ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower."﴾

﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me"﴾ — i.e., other than me, owing to its magnificence and greatness; a gift of bounty and a preference of favour: ﴿Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[36] ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, running by his command gently, wherever he willed.﴾

﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾ means: We made it subservient to his obedience, answering his supplication. ﴿Running by his command gently﴾ means: soft and easy, yet with force and strength. For this reason it is described in another verse as ﴿violent﴾ [al-Anbiya': 81]. ﴿Wherever he willed﴾ means: wherever he intended.

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, Exalted is He:

[37] ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver.﴾

﴿And the devils﴾ is in coordination (ʿaṭf) with "the wind" (in the preceding verse). ﴿Every builder and diver﴾, i.e., in the depths of the sea.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[38] ﴿And others bound together in shackles﴾.

﴿And others bound together in shackles﴾: that is, chained together in fetters, so that they are not sent forth to any work.

(p-٥١٠٤)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[39] ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold, without account.﴾

﴿This is Our gift, so bestow﴾: that is, upon whomever you wish, of the near ones and others. ﴿Or withhold﴾: that is, refrain. ﴿Without account﴾: that is, without being called to account for the bestowing or the withholding. So it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the concealed pronoun (al-mustakinn) in the verb, or it is a ḥāl relating to "gift" (ʿaṭāʾ), or it is a complement (ṣilah) of it, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ). The meaning: it is an abundant gift that can hardly be counted or limited. Great quantity is expressed by saying "it cannot be numbered," "it cannot be reckoned," and the like.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verse 40:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:

[40] ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is nearness and a good return.﴾

﴿And indeed, for him with Us is nearness﴾ means closeness in ranks, and ﴿a good return﴾ means a place of return in the Hereafter.

Note of caution:

The narrators of hadith (al-Athariyyun) have related here stories both long and short, agreeing and differing. Ibn Kathir said: "All of them are taken from the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and among them is a group who do not believe in the prophethood of Sulayman, peace be upon him. So it is apparent that they lie about him, and for this reason the context of these stories contains objectionable matters. Ibn Hajar's strengthening of some of them, on the ground that al-Nasa'i narrated it with a sound chain, carries no weight. The matter is not limited to the soundness of the chain alone, even if it were in the two Sahihs; so how about a report narrated by others than these two?"

Al-Razi mentioned that the stories narrated here belong to the people of mere verbal padding (ahl al-hashw) in their interpretation, while the people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) have their own interpretations, and he cited them, so refer to them.

Imam Ibn Hazm said: The meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We tested Sulayman﴾ [Sad: 34] is: We gave him of the kingdom that by which We tested his obedience, just as He, exalted is He, said confirming Musa, peace be upon him, in his saying: ﴿It is none but Your trial; You leave astray thereby whom You will and guide whom You will﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], since among trials is that by which Allah guides whom He wills. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Ankabut: 1] ﴿Do the people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tried?﴾ [al-Ankabut: 2] ﴿And We had already tried those before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-Ankabut: 3]. So this trial is testing, until the guided is distinguished from the astray. Thus Allah's trial of Sulayman is only His testing of him until his virtue became manifest, and nothing beyond this is but fables produced by the heretics of the Jews and their like.

As for the body placed upon his throne, Allah, exalted is He, has accomplished by it what He willed. We believe in this as it is, and we say: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has spoken truly; all is from our Lord." If a sound text came in the Qur'an, or from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explaining what this body is, we would hold to it. But if no text or sound report has come explaining what it is, then it is not lawful for anyone to speak by conjecture, which is the most false of speech regarding this, and he would be lying against Allah, Mighty and Majestic. However, we have no doubt whatsoever in the falsehood of the saying of one who said that he was a jinn who took his form, rather we are certain that it is a lie, and Allah, exalted is He, does not expose His Messenger (ﷺ) to such exposure. Likewise we reject the saying of one who said that he was a son of his, whom he sent to the clouds to be raised, for Sulayman, peace be upon him, was too knowledgeable to raise his son without what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had fixed in human nature of milk and food. All of these are fabricated, false fables, whose chains of transmission have never been sound at all. End of quote.

Al-Qashani claimed that the story of the jinn and the ring with Sulayman is among the fabrications of the Jewish sages, like the rest of what the sages placed in their parables, such as the tales of Absal and Salaman.

Then al-Qashani undertook to interpret it, but he resolved one difficulty with a greater difficulty, may Allah pardon him. He said before this: if the story is correct in its conformity to reality, then he was tested with the like of what Dhu al-Nun and Adam, peace be upon them both, were tested with. End of quote. And Allah knows best.

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[41] ﴿And remember Our servant Job, when he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾

﴿And remember﴾ i.e., in the context of trial and the good outcome of patience in it: ﴿Our servant﴾ i.e., the perfect one in realizing servitude (ʿubūdiyyah): ﴿Job, when he called out to his Lord﴾ i.e., he supplicated to Him and entreated Him, saying: ﴿"Indeed, Satan has touched me"﴾ i.e., has afflicted me: ﴿"with hardship"﴾ i.e., toil, (with a ḍammah on the nūn, and with a fatḥah with a sukūn on the ṣād, and with fatḥah or ḍammah on both): ﴿"and torment"﴾ i.e., severe pain. Then His words, Exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verse 42:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[42] ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool washing-place and a drink.﴾

﴿Strike with your foot﴾ is a narration of what his supplication (peace be upon him) was answered with. That is: We responded to him and said: Strike with your foot, i.e., run with it and walk, for you have been healed and cured of your illness, your body has grown strong, and your frame has become sound. ﴿This is a cool washing-place and a drink﴾, i.e., water with which you wash yourself and from which you drink. The indication is to a spring, or a river, or the like.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[43] ﴿And We gave him his family, and their like along with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding.﴾

﴿And We gave him his family﴾ by reuniting them with him after their separation. ﴿And their like along with them as a mercy from Us﴾, meaning, out of Our compassion for him, through this multiplying and blessing. ﴿And a reminder for those of understanding﴾, meaning: and a reminder for them, so that they may await relief through patience and attain their hope through true reliance (on God).

(p. 5107) **Allah the Exalted said:**

[44] ﴿And take in your hand a bundle of grass, and strike with it, and do not break your oath. Indeed, We found him patient. What an excellent servant! Indeed, he was one who turned back (to Allah) often.﴾

(p. 5107) ﴿And take in your hand a bundle﴾: a small bundle. ﴿and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾. ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾: in everything We tested him with. ﴿What an excellent servant! Indeed, he was one who turned back﴾: one who returned to Allah the Exalted often, through repentance, supplication and worship.

**Remarks:**

**First:** Ayyub (peace be upon him) was a prophet and a wealthy man, among the owners of land and livestock, and he was a leader among his people. His property and dwelling were in the southeast of the Dead Sea, between the lands of Edom and the Arabian desert. At that time the land was fertile and excellent in soil, with many flowing waters. His era came after the era of Ibrahim and before the era of Musa (peace be upon them all). This is what some researchers have verified. And Allah knows best.

**Second:** Many exegetes mention here narrations and stories from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives derived from Israelite sources) concerning his trial (peace be upon him). None of these, as a whole, is to be relied upon, except for their general outline, which is what the Noble Revelation indicated, because that is the certain part. It is that he (peace be upon him) was struck by a great affliction in his person, his property and his family, and that he endured this with a patience that became a proverbial example of his steadfastness, the breadth of his chest and his courage. And that he was rewarded for the good of his patience with multiplied recompense.

**Third:** Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why was the touch attributed to Satan, when it is not permissible for Allah to give Satan power over His prophets to fulfil his desire of exhausting and torturing them? And if he were able to do that, he would not have left any righteous person without afflicting him and destroying him. And it has been repeated in the Qur'an that he has no authority except whispering alone?

I say: Since his whispering to him, and his obedience to it in what he whispered, was a cause of the fatigue and punishment which Allah touched him with, he attributed it to him. He observed good manners in this, in that he did not attribute it to Allah in his supplication, even though Allah is its doer and no one is able to do it but Him. It was also said: he meant what Satan used to whisper to him during his illness, of magnifying the affliction that had befallen him, and urging him towards aversion and impatience. So he sought refuge with Allah the Exalted that He would suffice him against that by removing the affliction, or by granting him success in crushing it and repelling it through beautiful patience. End of quotation.

**Fourth:** The words of the Exalted, ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it﴾ and the verse, indicate that he (peace be upon him) had previously taken an oath. Here they have related reports about the thing sworn to, none of which is authentic. Allah knows best about it, and there is no need to explain it, since the purpose is to inform of another mercy and a second favour upon him, may the blessings of Allah be upon him. It is the indication of a way out of breaking the oath, through a concession and an easy, lenient method that removes hardship. Here we present the best of what has been written on the verse, so as to make the reader pause over it:

Al-Suyuti said in (*al-Iklil*): Ibn Abi Hatim related, through the chain of Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others, that Ayyub had sworn that he would flog his wife one hundred lashes. When Allah removed the affliction from him, he was commanded to take a bundle and strike her with it. So he took one hundred twigs and struck her with a single blow.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This ruling applies to this Community for whoever swears an oath similar to what Ayyub swore. Then he also related from Ata', who said: It is for people in general. And from Mujahid, who said: It was specific to Ayyub. Al-Kiya al-Harrasi said: al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Zufar held that whoever does this has fulfilled his oath, while Malik differed and considered it specific to Ayyub.

He said: The verse is evidence that a husband may strike his wife, and that he may swear an oath without making an exception.

End of quotation from *al-Iklil*.

This verse has been cited as evidence that the exception (*istithna'*) must be connected (to the oath), for if it were not a condition, He would have commanded him to make the exception, and there would have been no need for striking with the bundle. Ata' used the verse to deduce another question. Sa'id ibn Mansur related from him, with a sound chain, that a man said to him: "I intended not to clothe my wife with a sleeve until she stands at 'Arafa." He said: "Carry her on a donkey, then go and stand with her at 'Arafa." He said: "I only meant the day of 'Arafa." Ata' said: "When Ayyub swore that he would flog his wife one hundred lashes, he did not intend to strike her with the bundle; Allah only commanded him to take a bundle and strike her with it." Ata' said: "The Qur'an is only lessons." End of the words of *al-Iklil*.

Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) has refuted, in his book (*I'lam*... rather, *Ighathat al-Lahfan*), the use of this verse as evidence for the permissibility of legal stratagems (*hiyal*). His wording is: As for the saying of the Exalted to Ayyub (peace be upon him), ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾, it is strange that this verse should be cited against one who says: if he swore that he would beat him ten lashes, then gathered them and struck him with them (p. 5109) in a single blow, he would not have fulfilled his oath. This is the view of the companions of Abu Hanifa, Malik and the companions of Ahmad.

Al-Shafi'i said: If he knows that all of them touched him, he has fulfilled his oath; if he knows that they did not touch him, he has not fulfilled it; and if he is in doubt, he has not broken it. And if this were sufficient to fulfil the oath of the one who swears, it would also suffice for the adulterer, the slanderer and the drinker to be relieved of the number of blows, by gathering for him one hundred lashes or eighty and striking him with them in one blow. And this applies only in the case of illness, as Imam Ahmad said concerning the sick man who is liable to the prescribed punishment, who is struck with a cluster (*'uthkal*) that removes the prescribed punishment from him. He cited what he related from Abu Umama ibn Sahl, from Sa'id ibn Sa'd ibn Ubada, who said: "Among our sons there was a weak, deficient man. He startled the people of the house only when he was with a female slave of the household, and he was abusing her. He was a Muslim, so Sa'd raised his case to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'Strike him with his prescribed punishment.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah! He is weaker than that; if we strike him one hundred times, we shall kill him.' He said: 'Then take for him a cluster containing one hundred twigs, strike him with a single blow, and let him go.'"

As for the story of Ayyub, it contains a subtle jurisprudence. His wife, out of her intense eagerness for his health and his recovery from his illness, used to seek a remedy for him with what was in her power. When Satan met her and said what he said, she informed Ayyub (peace be upon him) of that, and he said: "It is Satan." Then he swore that if Allah the Exalted healed him, he would strike her one hundred lashes. She was thus excused and well-intentioned concerning his affair, and there was no expiation (*kaffara*) in their law. For if there had been an expiation in their law, he would have turned to it and would not have needed to strike her. So the oath, in their view, was binding like the prescribed punishments (*hudud*).

It is established that the one liable to the prescribed punishment, if he is excused, is given relief, by gathering for him one hundred twigs or one hundred lashes and striking him with them in a single blow. Ayyub's wife was excused; she did not know that the one who addressed her was Satan, and she only intended kindness. So she did not deserve punishment. Therefore Allah gave His Prophet Ayyub (peace be upon him) a ruling that he should treat her as one who is excused. This was in addition to her gentleness towards him and her kindness to him. Thus he combined fulfilling his oath with kindness towards his wife, who was well-intentioned and excused and did not deserve punishment. It thereby becomes clear that the text of the Qur'an in the story of Ayyub (peace be upon him) agrees with the text of the Sunna concerning the weak man who committed fornication. So these two cases should not be extended beyond their proper places.

(p. 5110) If it is said: then say the same of one who swore that he would strike his wife or his female slave one hundred times, and they were both excused and blameless, that he fulfils his oath by gathering that into striking them with one hundred twigs. It is said: Allah has provided him a way out through expiation, and it is obligatory for him to expiate his oath. Allah decides that fulfilling the oath is right here, but it is not lawful for him to fulfil it in this way; rather, his fulfilling it is breaking it, together with the expiation. And it is not lawful for him to strike her, whether separately or gathered together.

If it is said: then when the striking is obligatory like the prescribed punishment, do you say it benefits him? It is said: Either the excuse is one whose removal is expected, such as extreme heat, extreme cold, or a slight illness; in that case its removal is awaited, and then he applies the obligatory prescribed punishment, as Muslim related in his *Sahih* from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): that a female slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) committed fornication, and he commanded me to flog her. I went to her and found that she was recently delivered of postnatal bleeding, so I feared that if I flogged her I would kill her. I mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "You did well; leave her until she recovers." End of the words of Ibn al-Qayyim.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[45] ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men of power and vision.﴾

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men of power and vision.﴾ That is: possessors of strength in worship and of reflection in knowing God, exalted is He. Al-Qashani said: That is, of action and knowledge, since the first is attributed to the hands and the second to sight and contemplation; and they are the masters of the perfections both practical and theoretical.

Al-Shihab said: ﴿al-aydi﴾ ("the hands") is a metaphor for strength, a mursal metaphor (majaz mursal). And "al-absar" ("the sight") is the plural of basar in the sense of basirah (insight), and this is also a metaphor, but it is well established in that sense. If by ﴿al-aydi﴾ is meant deeds, then it is mention of the cause with the intended effect (dhikr al-sabab wa iradat al-musabbab). And "al-absar" in the sense of insights is a metaphor for the knowledge that branches from them, just like the first. And on both interpretations, there is an allusion (ta'ridh) that whoever is not like this has no limb and no sight. End of quote.

[ (p-٥١١١) ] On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[46] ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: the remembrance of the Abode.﴾

﴿Indeed, We purified them﴾ means: We cleansed them of the admixture of the qualities of the souls and the turbidity of their appetites, and made them sincerely Ours through true love. ﴿With a pure [quality]: the remembrance of the Abode﴾ means: the everlasting abode and the original dwelling-place. That is, We chose them for Our sake because of their remembrance of the world of holiness and their turning away from the source of defilement, facing toward Our lights, with no inclination at all toward this world or its darknesses.

A subtle point:

Al-Samin said: Nafi' and Hisham read ﴿بِخالِصَةٍ ذِكْرى الدّارِ﴾ with the idafa (genitive construction, إضافة). There are several possibilities for it:

The first: he made khāliṣa (خالصة, "pure") an idafa to dhikrā (ذكرى, "remembrance") as a clarifying genitive (لِلْبَيانِ), because the pure thing may be a remembrance or other than a remembrance, as in His saying, ﴿بِشِهابٍ قَبَسٍ﴾ [al-Naml: 7], since a flaming brand may be a firebrand or other than one.

The second: khāliṣa is a verbal noun (مَصْدَر) meaning ikhlāṣ (إخلاص, "sincerity"), so it is a verbal noun idafa'd to its object (مَفْعُول), with the agent omitted. That is: "by their sincerely remembering the Abode, and forgetting, when it is mentioned, the remembrance of the world." Verbal nouns have also come in the pattern fā'ila, as in ʿāqiba (عاقبة, "outcome"). Alternatively, the meaning is: "by Our sincerely granting them the remembrance of the Abode."

The rest of the readers read it with tanwin (تنوين, nunation) and without idafa, and there are several possibilities for this:

The first: it is a verbal noun meaning ikhlāṣ, so dhikrā is in the accusative (مَنصُوبًا) governed by it. It may also mean khulūṣ (خُلوص, "purity"), in which case dhikrā is in the nominative (مَرْفُوعًا) governed by it. A verbal noun can govern its object whether it is nunated or idafa'd. Alternatively, khāliṣa is an active participle (اسم فاعل) in its usual sense. Then dhikrā is a substitute (بَدَل) for it, or an explanatory apposition (بَيان) to it, or it is in the accusative by an implied "I mean" (أَعْنِي), or it is in the nominative by an implied subject (مُبْتَدَأ). Al-Dār (الدار, "the Abode") may be the direct object of dhikrā, or an adverbial complement (ظَرْف), either by extension (على الاتساع) or by dropping the preposition (إسقاط الخافض). If khāliṣa is an adjective, then it modifies an omitted noun, that is: "by means of a pure quality." End.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[47, 48] ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent.﴾ ﴿And mention Ismail, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl, and all are among the excellent.﴾ [Sad: 48].

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen﴾ — that is, those selected from among the people of their kind because of their nearness to Us. ﴿The excellent﴾ — that is, those purified of the taints of evil. It is the plural of "khayr" (good), the opposite of "sharr" (evil), which is an elative form (af'al al-tafdil). Or it is the plural of "khayyir," the intensified form, or of its lightened form.

﴿And mention Ismail, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl, and all are among the excellent﴾ [Sad: 48] — that is, with prophethood and messengerhood, for guidance and reform. "Al-Yasa'" is the successor of Ilyas, and he was his servant. In Hebrew he is called "Elisha'," just as Ilyas is called "Elijah" in it. In the Torah there is a lengthy account about al-Yasa', his prophethood, and his miracles, may the blessings of Allah be upon him. The knowledge of the reports of these prophets, peace be upon them, has already been mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[49, 50] ﴿This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return. Gardens of perpetual residence, their doors opened for them.﴾ [Sad: 50].

﴿This is a reminder﴾ means: it is an honour for them. And (al-dhikr, "the reminder") is used here figuratively for the honour itself. Al-Shihab said: because honour entails renown and being remembered among people, so it is used figuratively to mean honour, by the relation of necessary association (ʿalaqat al-luzum). The meaning is therefore: in the mention of their stories and in Allah's praise of them there is honour for them. Al-Zamakhshari preferred that the meaning is: this is a kind of reminder, which is the Qur'an; that is, the tanwin (nunation) is for classification (lil-tanwi'). The intended "reminder" is the Qur'an, and its mention is only for the transition from one type of speech to another.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When He had continued and completed the mention of the prophets, which is one of the sections of revelation and one of its kinds, and He wished to mention after it another section, namely the mention of Paradise and its people, He said: ﴿This is a reminder﴾ (p-5113) ﴿And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [Sad: 50], that is, abiding and eternity; ﴿their doors opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50], that is, whenever they come to them, they find them open, awaiting them.

Al-Zamakhshari preferred that the meaning is: this is a kind of reminder, which is the Qur'an; that is, the tanwin (nunation) is for classification (lil-tanwi'). The intended "reminder" is the Qur'an, and its mention is only for the transition from one type of speech to another.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When He had continued and completed the mention of the prophets, which is one of the sections of revelation and one of its kinds, and He wished to mention after it another section, namely the mention of Paradise and its people, He said: ﴿This is a reminder﴾ (p-5113) ﴿And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [Sad: 50], that is, abiding and eternity; ﴿their doors opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50], that is, whenever they come to them, they find them open, awaiting them.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[51] ﴿Reclining therein, they call therein for abundant fruit and drink.﴾

﴿Reclining therein⦆ means: upon couches. ﴿They call therein for abundant fruit and drink⦆ means: whatever they ask for, they find, and it is brought as they desire.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verse 52:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[52] ﴿And with them will be maidens restraining their glances, equal in age.﴾

﴿And with them will be maidens restraining their glances﴾: meaning, they do not look at anyone other than their husbands. Or, the glance of the husbands prevents them from looking at others, due to the intensity of their beauty. This is more eloquent. Or it means women with large, lustrous eyes (ḥūr al-ṭarf), the plural of ahwar (having very white eyes with dark irises), and a veiled pearl is likened to the ḥawārī (the white flour or pure white garment) in its whiteness and purity. ﴿Equal in age﴾: meaning, they are of equal age and rank, with no old woman among them. Atrāb is the plural of tirb (pl. atrāb), with a kasra and then a sukūn, and it is the one born with another at the same time, as if the two fell upon the turāb (dust) at one time. So tirb is a form meaning mufā'il (companion) and mutārib (one of the same age). And kamithl means "in the sense of" mumāthil (equal, similar).

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[53] ﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning.﴾

﴿This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾: i.e., for the time of its recompense. The lam (ل) is causal (taʿlīliyyah). For what He promised them is on account of their obedience and their righteous deeds, and these become manifest through the Reckoning and take place after it. So it is treated as though it were the cause for the fulfilment of the promise being contingent upon it, and the attribution to the Day and the Reckoning is therefore figurative (majāzī). But if the lam is taken in the sense of "after" (baʿda), as in "a letter was written for five [nights]" (kutiba li-khams), it is free of what has been mentioned. This is what al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) conveyed.

(p-5114) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[54] ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end.﴾

﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end.﴾ I.e., no cessation.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verses 55–56:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55, 56] ﴿This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return. Hell, which they will burn in, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Sad: 56].

﴿This﴾ means: this is a section describing Paradise and its people. So it is the subject (mubtada') of an elided predicate (khabar muqaddar), or the matter is "this," so it is the predicate of an elided word, or the object (maf'ul) of an elided word: ﴿And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return. Hell, which they will burn in, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Sad: 56], that is, al-mihad (the resting place, the bed), a metaphor taken from the bed of the sleeper.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verses 55–56:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55, 56] ﴿This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return. Hell, which they will burn in, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Sad: 56].

﴿This﴾ means: this is a section describing Paradise and its people. Hell, which they will burn in, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Sad: 56], that is, al-mihad (the resting place, the bed), a metaphor taken from the bed of the sleeper.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verse 57:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words:

[57] ﴿This! So let them taste it: boiling water and ghassaq.﴾

﴿This! So let them taste it: boiling water and ghassaq.﴾ Ghassaq is what flows from the pus of the people of the Fire; that is, what drips and flows. The clause ﴿so let them taste it﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) between the subject (mubtada') and its predicate (khabar).

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[58] ﴿And other punishments of similar kind, in pairs.﴾

﴿And other﴾ means: and something else that is tasted, or another punishment, ﴿of similar kind﴾, meaning: of this tasted thing, or of the punishment, in its severity and humiliation; ﴿in pairs﴾, meaning: of kinds and categories. Then He explained what is said to the tyrannical leaders when they are made to enter the Fire.

(p-٥١١٥)The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[59] ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you; no welcome for them. Indeed, they are the ones who will burn in the Fire.﴾

﴿This is a troop rushing in with you﴾: that is, this is a host of your followers and your likes, people of evil natures and various vices, rushing in with you into the narrow straits of humiliation and the entrances of disgrace. Iqtiham (rushing in) is to take on hardship and to enter into it. His words ﴿no welcome for them﴾: that is, a supplication from the leaders against their followers. Or it is a description of "troop" (fawj). Or it is a circumstantial clause, meaning: said about them, ﴿no welcome for them﴾, that is, they came to their Lord without any spaciousness or ease, because of the severity of their punishment, their being in constriction and distress, and some of them feeling estranged from others, due to the ugliness of the sights and the evil of the tidings. ﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will burn in the Fire﴾: that is, they will enter it because of their deeds, just as we will.

The Interpretation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[60] ﴿They will say: "Nay, it is you! There is no welcome for you! You have brought this upon us, so what an evil abode it is!"﴾

﴿They will say﴾, that is, the followers say to the leaders: ﴿Nay, it is you! There is no welcome for you!﴾ That is, rather you are more deserving of what you said, because your punishment is doubled on account of your own misguidance and your leading others astray. ﴿You have brought this upon us﴾, that is, you put forward the punishment for us by leading us astray and seducing us.

Al-Qasimi said: These exchanges may take place by the tongue of speech, or by the tongue of circumstance, since the expression is not restricted to literal meaning; however, the more apparent is the first, and this is supported by His words, exalted be He, after this: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. ﴿So what an evil abode it is!﴾ That is, the place of settlement is Jahannam.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase him in doubled punishment in the Fire."﴾

﴿They said﴾, i.e., the followers as well: ﴿"Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase him in doubled punishment in the Fire"﴾, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Our Lord, give them double the punishment"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68].

"The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:

[62] ﴿And they will say, "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the bad?"﴾

﴿And they said﴾, i.e., the tyrants (al-tāghūn), or the followers (al-atbā'): ﴿"What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the bad?"﴾, meaning the poor among the Muslims, whom they belittled and mocked."

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[63] ﴿Did We take them as a laughingstock, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾

﴿Did We take them as a laughingstock?﴾ It is read with the form of a declarative statement, in which case it is an attribute of "men" (rijālan). It is also read with the interrogative hamzah, in which case it is a denial by themselves and a rebuke to themselves for having mocked them. As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾, meaning: they inclined away from them in arrogance and withdrew from them out of disdain. The meaning is: which of the two actions did we take toward them, mocking them or belittling them? This is a denial of both matters by themselves, expressing regret and remorse over what they did and over the terrible punishment that befell them alone. It has also been said that "am" (or) here carries the meaning of "bal" (rather), that is: rather, our eyes have turned away from them because of the concealment of their place from us in the Fire, as if they were consoling themselves with the impossible, saying: "Perhaps they are with us in Hell, but our sight has not fallen upon them." Then, at that point, they will know that they are in the lofty ranks, and this is His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire, "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" They will say, "Yes." Then a caller will proclaim between them, "The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-A'raf: 44] up to His words ﴿"Enter the Garden"﴾ [al-A'raf: 49], and the verse. It has also been said that "am" carries the meaning of "bal" as well, that is: rather, our eyes have turned away from them because they are in another abode, which is the abode of bliss. It is also read as "sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin and with a kasra.

(p-5117) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[64] ﴿Indeed, that is the truth: the dispute of the people of the Fire.﴾

﴿Indeed, that﴾ means: that which was related about them, ﴿is the truth: the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾, meaning: it is certainly occurring and established. And ﴿the dispute﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿truth﴾, or the predicate of an omitted subject. It was also read in the accusative case as a substitute for ﴿that﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "Why did He call that a dispute?" I say: He likened their mutual speech, and the questions and answers that passed between them, to what takes place between disputants of that kind; and because the saying of the leaders, ﴿No welcome to them﴾ [Sad: 59], and the saying of their followers, ﴿Rather, no welcome to you﴾ [Sad: 60], belong to the category of contention. So He called all of that speech a dispute, because it includes that. End of quote.

Al-Nasir wrote in the margin on it: This confirms what preceded, that His saying, ﴿No welcome to them; indeed, they are the ones who will burn in the Fire﴾ [Sad: 59], is the speech of the arrogant disbelievers.

And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Rather, no welcome to you﴾ [Sad: 60], is the speech of the followers. Thus the contention, on this interpretation, arises from both parties, and the dispute is thereby realized. This is contrary to those who said that the first is the speech of the keepers of Hell and the second is the speech of the followers; for on that reading the dispute would come only from one of the two groups. The first explanation is therefore more likely and more firmly established. End of quote.

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[65] ﴿Say, "I am only a warner, and there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Subduer."﴾

﴿Say, "I am only a warner"﴾ meaning: a messenger who instils fear. ﴿And there is no deity except Allah, the One﴾ meaning: without offspring and without partner. ﴿The Subduer﴾ meaning: the One who prevails over His creation.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[66] ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Mighty, the Oft-Forgiving.﴾

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ i.e., of the creatures and the wonders [contained in them]. ﴿The Mighty﴾ i.e., the One who is not overcome when He punishes the disobedient. ﴿The Oft-Forgiving﴾ i.e., to whoever repents and turns back in penitence.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[67] ﴿Say: It is a momentous news.﴾

"﴿Say, it is﴾": that is, the matter about which I warned you, namely the Tawhid (Oneness of God), and the sending of the Messenger with it: ﴿a momentous news.﴾

The discussion of the Almighty's words:

[68] ﴿You turn away from it.﴾

﴿You turn away from it﴾ means: because of the persistence of your heedlessness. For the intelligent person does not turn away from the likes of this. How could he, when clear proofs have been established against him? As for the Oneness (tawhid) of God, there are the traces of His power and His wondrous creation that have passed. As for the sending of His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, with it, [there is] His saying:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[69] ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they were disputing.﴾

﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they were disputing.﴾ That is: his report of the discourse of the angels and what passed between them, as it is related in the previous Scriptures, without having heard it or studied a book, cannot be conceived except through revelation.

Al-Qashani said: He distinguished between the disputing of the Exalted Assembly and the disputing of the people of the Fire, by His saying concerning the disputing of the people of the Fire: ﴿Indeed, that is true﴾ [Sad: 64], and concerning the disputing of the Exalted Assembly: ﴿when they were disputing﴾, because that [the disputing of the people of the Fire] is real and never ends in agreement, whereas this [the disputing of the angels] is incidental, arising from their lack of knowledge of the perfection of Adam, peace be upon him, which is above their perfections, and it ended in agreement when they said: ﴿Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33], as is mentioned in al-Baqarah at the interpretation of this story. End of quote.

In sum, the disputing mentioned in the verse is the one alluded to in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Al-Razi said: This is the best of what has been said about it.

Then he said: If it is asked, how was the angels' disputing with Him, Exalted is He, permissible? We say: there is no doubt that a question and answer took place there, and that resembles disputing and debate, and resemblance is a cause for the permissibility of metaphor; therefore for this reason the term "disputing" was fittingly applied to it. End of quote.

Its summary: ﴿yakhtasimun﴾ ("they dispute") is a sequential (tab'iyyah) metaphor for ﴿yataqawalun﴾ ("they speak to one another"). It has also been said: the meaning of the verse is the negation of knowledge of the unseen from him, peace be upon him, and the rejection of their suggestion that he inform them of what occurs in the Exalted Assembly of disputing, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "I do not tell you that I have the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen"﴾ [al-An'am: 50], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Knowledge is only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner"﴾ [al-Mulk: 26]. Therefore He said after this:

**On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[70] ﴿Only what is revealed to me comes to me, and I am only a clear warner.﴾

﴿Only what is revealed to me comes to me, and I am only a clear warner.﴾ It is also read *innama* with a kasra (*inna*), as a direct quotation (*hikayah*).

**Remarks:**

**First:** Al-Razi said: Know that His saying, ﴿You turn away from it﴾ [Sad 68], is an encouragement to reflection (*nazar*) and reasoned inference (*istidlal*), and a prohibition of blind imitation (*taqlid*). These matters are noble and lofty concerns, for if a person is upon the truth regarding them, he attains the greatest gates of happiness, and if he is upon falsehood regarding them, he falls into the greatest gates of wretchedness. Thus these inquiries are great tidings and lofty, sublime matters, and sound reason requires that a person approach them with complete caution, and not be content with laxity and leniency.

**Second:** We have previously mentioned that most of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) interpret the dispute (*ikhtisam*) as a contention about the matter of Adam, peace be upon him, with the angels. It has also been said that their dispute is their debate among themselves in deriving knowledge, just as debate takes place among the people of knowledge on earth. This was related by al-Karmani in his *Ajaib*.

Ibn Kathir held that it refers to what occurred concerning Adam, peace be upon him, the refusal of Iblis to prostrate to him, and his contention with his Lord regarding his preference over him. He held that His saying, exalted is He, afterward, ﴿When your Lord said﴾ [Sad 71], is an explanation of it. I have not seen this transmitted from anyone. Rather, what is transmitted from Ibn Abbas and others is what has preceded: that it concerns Adam and the angels. All of this rests on affirming knowledge of the dispute through revelation, with the implied meaning: "I would have had no knowledge of it, were it not for the revelation." Do not forget the other view as well, and the noble wording applies to all of these without contradiction. And Allah knows best.

The mention of the dispute of the Exalted Assembly (*al-mala' al-a'la*) has come in the hadith of Imam Ahmad from Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delayed us one morning from the dawn prayer, until we nearly saw the rising of the sun's horn. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out quickly, called the iqamah (the second call to prayer), prayed, and shortened his prayer. When he finished the salam, he said, (ﷺ): 'Remain as you are.' Then he turned toward us and said: 'I stood in the night and prayed what was decreed for me, then I dozed during my prayer until I awoke, and behold, I was with my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, in the best of forms. He said: O Muhammad! Do you know about what the Exalted Assembly is disputing?' I said: 'I do not know, O Lord!' He repeated it three times. Then I saw Him place His palm between my shoulders until I felt the coolness of His fingertips between my chest. Then everything was made manifest to me, and I knew. He said: O Muhammad! About what is the Exalted Assembly disputing? I said: 'About the expiations (*kaffarat*).' He said: 'And what are the expiations?' I said: 'Walking on foot to the congregations, sitting in the mosques after the prayers, and completing the ablution in hardship.' He said: 'And what are the degrees?' I said: 'Feeding food, gentle speech, and praying while people sleep.' He said: 'Ask.' I said: 'O Allah! I ask You for doing good deeds, abandoning evil deeds, love of the poor, that You forgive me and have mercy on me, and when You intend a trial for a people, take me to You without being tried. I ask You for Your love, the love of those who love You, and the love of a deed that brings me closer to Your love.'" And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, it is true, so study it and teach it."

Ibn Kathir said: This is the well-known hadith of the dream. Whoever takes it to be a waking experience has erred. It is found in the Sunan collections through several chains, and this same hadith has been transmitted by al-Tirmidhi from the narration of Jahdam ibn Abdullah al-Yamami, and he said: "Hasan sahih" (good and authentic).

Then Ibn Kathir said: This dispute mentioned here is not the dispute mentioned in the Qur'an, for this has already been explained. As for the dispute mentioned in the Qur'an, it is explained after this. End of quote. He means His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[71, 72] ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] spirit, then fall down to him in prostration."﴾ [Sad: 72]

﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay"﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] spirit, then fall down to him in prostration﴾ [Sad: 72]. That is: fall down to him in prostration, in veneration and honor, when I have made his creation proportionate and given him life by breathing the spirit into him. "Fa-idha" (so when) is a substitute (badal) for the first "idh" (when), detailing what was left general before it concerning the dispute. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn Kathir followed him. Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "udhkur" (mention), and this is the more apparent view in my opinion, and the second statement regarding the preceding verse supports it.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 38, verses 73–74:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[73, 74] ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely,﴾ ﴿except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers.﴾ [Sad: 74].

[73, 74] ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely,﴾ ﴿except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers.﴾ [Sad: 74].
